title: Position measurement of a levitated particle with vectorial light
authors: Daniel Tandeitnik, Lucas Bianchi, Sebastian Gutierrez-Bernal, Joanna A. Zielińska, Paulo A. Maia Neto, Thiago Guerreiro
abstract: We develop a fully vectorial, semiclassical scattering formalism for optically levitated dipolar scatterers, expressed within the angular spectrum representation and applicable to arbitrary trapping-field configurations as well as to high--numerical-aperture focusing. Within this framework, we introduce the information radiation pattern to characterize the angular distribution of position-dependent information and use a Richards--Wolf projection of the scattered field onto the local-oscillator mode to quantify the resulting mode-matching efficiency, yielding experimentally realistic forward- and backward-detection efficiencies. As a worked example, we apply the formalism to a radially polarized trapping beam and confirm that the axial recoil heating rate is reduced relative to a conventional linearly polarized Gaussian tweezer. The theoretical framework is implemented in LevitationToolbox, an open-source Python package intended to support the design and optimization of near-Heisenberg-limited levitated optomechanical experiments.
summary: The paper introduces a comprehensive, fully vectorial theory to analyze how position measurements are limited by photon scattering noise in levitated nanoparticles. By using the Angular Spectrum Representation, it accurately models non-paraxial effects, demonstrating that structured light like radial polarization can suppress unwanted axial backaction forces compared to standard Gaussian traps.
main_problem: To develop a fully vectorial, semiclassical formalism for characterizing position measurement backaction noise and detection efficiency in optically levitated dipolar scatterers.
main_result: The vectorial approach shows that structured light fields, such as radially polarized beams, can fundamentally suppress axial measurement backaction compared to conventional Gaussian traps.
method: The authors use the angular spectrum representation (ASR) within a semiclassical scattering formalism to calculate momentum transfer and detection efficiency, moving beyond paraxial approximations.
model_or_system: The system involves levitating mesoscopic nanoparticles trapped by arbitrary optical fields. The theoretical model incorporates Langevin dynamics and treats the measurement process using photon shot noise statistics.
key_observables: Information radiation pattern, mode-matching efficiency ($\eta_{det,q}$), backaction force spectral density ($S_{b,k,q}$), and the resulting effective imprecision noise ($\Delta x_{	ext{eff}}$).
important_parameters: The generalized geometric factor ($	ext{C}_q$), filling factor ($f_0$), and the comparison between linearly vs. radially polarized beams.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the Rayleigh scattering regime ($a \ll \lambda$) and employs a semiclassical treatment for the trapping field, while using ASR to handle non-paraxial effects.
figures_summary: Figures compare optomechanical parameters (like backaction rates) for different polarizations as a function of beam filling factor, highlighting differences between vectorial and paraxial approximations.
paper_structure: The paper builds from developing the general vectorial scattering formalism using ASR to calculate momentum transfer ($	ext{C}_q$), then applies this framework to quantify detection efficiency ($\eta_{det,q}$), culminating in specific examples comparing Gaussian versus radially polarized traps.
why_interesting: This work provides advanced theoretical tools for designing next-generation quantum sensors by rigorously accounting for the polarization and angular structure of light fields on measurement backaction limits.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematic representation of coherent photon scatter- ing and position detection in an optical levitation setup. The trapping beam (propagating left to right) is strongly focused by a high-NA objective. The levitated nanoparticle acts as a driven point-dipole, interacting with an incident photon (wavevector ki) and scattering it into a final state (wavevec- tor kf). The resulting dipole radiation pattern carries the particle’s spatial information into the far-field. This coherent signal is subsequently gathered either by the trapping objec- tive (backward detection) or by a secondary collection lens (forward detection) for phase-sensitive measurement.
